draftSource.title: Nephrite origins of ancient jade artifacts from the Houtaomuga site in Northeast China (2026)

f the Houtaomuga site and related Neolithic cultural sites and nephrite deposits.
Full size image
A Distribution of major Neolithic cultural sites and straight-line distances from Houtaomuga to known white nephrite deposits in Northeast Asia. B Location of the Houtaomuga site. Cultural sites shown include Xinglongwa, Hongshan and the Glazkovo cultural horizon; mapped nephrite deposits include Chuncheon, Xiuyan and the Baikal region. Base map in A adapted from Natural Earth (www.naturalearthdata.com; public domain). B Adapted from Jing et al. (2023).
Excavations at Houtaomuga have identified seven phases, of which Phases I–IV correspond to Neolithic culture16. Eleven jade artifacts have been reported from these phases, most of which belong to Phases III–IV. Based on radiocarbon (14C) dating and comparison with other Neolithic archaeological cultures in the region17, Phases I–IV are tentatively dated to 8000–5000 BP, with Phase III assigned to 6500–5500 BP and Phase IV to 5500–5000 BP18,19,20.
Nine jade artifacts unearthed from Phases III–IV were selected for analyses (Fig. 2, and Table 1), including six intact artifacts and three fragments. The samples are generally small and thin. Six artifacts are white and transparent to semi-transparent, whereas three fragments are grey-yellowish green and translucent. All nine samples have ground and polished surfaces, and many of them retain traces of natural weathering such as residual cortex, pits and minor fractures. Basic information on colour, specific gravity, transparency, object type, size, drilling technique, presence or absence of flat surfaces and excavation date of each sample is summarised in Table 1.

Two perforations are present: an upper hole (2.2 mm) with straight, smoothly polished walls, and a larger lower aperture (11.5 mm) whose walls show regularly spaced grinding striations (Fig. 3c). Similarly, regularly arranged grinding marks are also visible within the concave area surrounding the upper perforation (Fig. 3b). The surfaces are evenly polished and retain localised fine scratches (Fig. 3d). Analytical methods
Because the artifacts are irreplaceable archaeological materials, four non-destructive analytical methods were used: microscopic inspection, physical-property measurements, Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy and Raman spectroscopy. All measurements were taken on exposed jade surfaces free of visible consolidants or thick soil crusts.
Visual inspection and physical-property measurements
Macroscopic observation under reflected light using a gemological microscope was carried out to record colour, transparency, weathering features, fractures, polishing traces, perforations and other technological characteristics of the artifacts. Selected surface areas were then examined at higher magnification to document the distribution of weathering pits and surface deposits.
Relative density (specific gravity, SG) was measured using the water-immersion (hydrostatic) method with deionised water at room temperature.
FTIR spectroscopy
FTIR spectra were obtained using a TENSOR27 Fourier-transform infrared spectrometer at the Gemmology Laboratory of China University of Geosciences, Beijing (CUGB). Measurements were conducted in reflectance mode with a spectral resolution of 4 cm−1 over the range of 400–1300 cm−1, and each spectrum was obtained by averaging 16 scans. Characteristic absorption bands were identified and each spectrum was compared with published reference data for tremolite-dominant nephrite19,20.
Raman spectroscopy
Raman spectra were acquired using a HR-Evolution micro-Raman spectrometer at the same laboratory, equipped with a 532 nm excitation laser and a 600 lines/mm grating. Spectra were recorded over the range 200–3700 cm−1. The laser power was set to 100%, with a laser spot diameter of approximately 1 μm, a spectral resolution of about 1 cm−1. Results
Macroscopic features
Based on overall morphology and surface characteristics, the jade artifacts were divided into two types with clear visual contrasts. Type I includes six artifacts that are white to greyish-white and transparent to semi-transparent but without flat faces, whereas Type II consists of three pieces that are grey-yellowish green and translucent and show one or more intentionally cut flat surfaces (Fig. 2).
Type I artifacts generally display weathered surfaces. Four samples (12DHAIIIM92①:7, 11DHAIIIF6②:1, 15DHAIM016②:2, 12DHAIIIM92①:5) show weathering characteristics on both sides, whereas two (13DHAIH019①:4, 13DHAIM010①:3) exhibit weathering characteristics on only one side, with the opposite face showing grinding traces but no cutting marks. Weathering features observed on Type I samples include brownish surface colouration, rounded or slightly weathered edges, small fractures, abrasions and pits of varying sizes (Figs. 3–8).

erved at the upper end. One side of the inner wall is smoothly polished with regularly arranged striations, whereas the opposite wall is fractured and irregular (Fig. 7b). One face is well preserved, showing fine, regularly arranged polishing marks and scattered small pits (Fig. 7c), whereas the opposite face bears a large fracture surface in the central area, covering roughly 30% of that side (Fig. 7d).
Sample 13DHAIM010①:3 (Fig. 8) is a dagger-shaped pendant, white and transparent, with no through-going cracks. Both faces are evenly polished. A circular perforation at the upper end (3.1 mm in diameter) has smoothly finished inner walls (Fig. 8c), and clear polishing striations are visible on the polished surface adjacent to the perforation (Fig. 8b). Yellow-brown to brown surface deposits occur along the rim (Fig. 8d). The surfaces bear scattered weathering pits (0.1–0.5 mm) and occasional dark-brown deposits, and a small fracture surface (approximately 1.0 × 0.2 mm) is present at the lower end (Fig. 8a, b).
Sample 12DHAIIIH057①:3 (Fig. 9) is a rectangular fragment. Both ends show flat fracture surfaces with no perforations. One side preserves parallel polishing marks (Fig. 9b). Roughly 60% of the upper surface is covered by a grey-brown clay accretion with an irregular and undulating margin (Fig. 9c). Exposed areas of jade are grey-yellowish green and semi-translucent to opaque, preserving localised polish sheen and small weathering pits (Fig. 9d).
Sample 14DHAIF010①:3 (Fig. 10) is an irregular triangular fragment. Both faces are evenly polished and display a grey-yellowish green and semi-translucent appearance. The fracture edge is irregular and serrated, exposing fresh jade material (Fig. 10a). Clear polishing striations are visible on the polished surface (Fig. 10b), and yellow-white depositional residues occur along the edge (Fig. 10a).
Sample 12DHAIVF4②:6 (Fig. 11) is a square fragment, grey-yellowish green and semi-translucent. The surfaces are smoothly polished, with no evidence of perforations or tooling grooves (Fig. 11a). One face bears an elliptical pattern of yellow to ochre surface deposits with a well-defined boundary (Fig. 11b).
Physical properties
Relative density (specific gravity, SG) was measured using the water-immersion method (Table 1). SG for Sample 7 (12DHAIIIH057①:3) could not be obtained because a soil crust adheres firmly to the surface. Excluding this case, the remaining seven artifacts yield SG values between 2.90 and 2.96 (mean = 2.94).

Two perforations are present: an upper hole (2.2 mm) with straight, smoothly polished walls, and a larger lower aperture (11.5 mm) whose walls show regularly spaced grinding striations (Fig. 3c). Similarly, regularly arranged grinding marks are also visible within the concave area surrounding the upper perforation (Fig. 3b). The surfaces are evenly polished and retain localised fine scratches (Fig. 3d). Yellow-brown surface deposits and small weathering pits are distributed around the perforations and along the rim (Fig. 3a).

The inner wall of the circular aperture is smoothly polished, and several small pits are distributed along the rim (Fig. 4c). Along the outer edge, shallow depressions measuring approximately 0.3–0.6 mm occur together with small surface deposits (Fig. 4d).

Type I and Type II exhibit two different sets of material and manufacturing logics. According to macroscopic observations, Type I pieces are generally small, thin, and locally transparent, and preserve natural break surfaces, brownish weathering bands and unevenly distributed corrosion pits. On the polished faces, brownish deposits and small pits were likely attributable to natural weathering26, natural breakage and surface weathering in shallow or near-surface settings27,28, indicating that the raw materials were originally small and irregular prior to working. Considering the limitations of Neolithic mining technologies, the raw materials for Type I were most likely obtained from easily accessible shallow nephrite outcrops.
The persistence of natural pits and brownish weathered zones on Type I pieces further indicates that a strategy of “working with the material” already existed. It can be envisaged that, given the size constraints of the raw material, Neolithic jade-workers tended to follow the natural shape of the stone. Perforations on Type I pieces were inferred to have been produced by double-sided drilling29, as evidenced by the biconical profiles together with fine, continuous grinding striations on the inner walls. This strategy, together with the perforations, clearly indicates careful control over tool alignment and the applied force during manufacture. In contrast, Type II pieces are grey-yellowish green and translucent, with a homogeneous texture, flat and regular polished faces, few weathering features and relatively regular fracture surfaces. These characteristics are more consistent with fragments cut from larger blocks or pre-shaped roughouts, suggesting that Type II pieces may represent by-products of semi-finished items within regional exchange networks30. In this context, the contrast between Type I and Type II provides a basis for discussing raw-material acquisition and working practices within the community: jade procurement and use were likely supported by multiple sources, involving different supply routes and different circulation stages.
With respect to the potential sources, the Baikal region was first considered because of its rich white nephrite resources and the occurrence of large white-nephrite rings associated with the Early Bronze Age Glazkovo cultural horizon31,32. However, Baikal nephrite is unlikely to account for the Houtaomuga material. Baikal white nephrite is typically slightly translucent to opaque and relatively coarse in texture33, and it often shows mosaic or “orange-peel” surface features34,35, in contrast to the fine-grained, white to greyish-white, transparent to semi-transparent appearance of Type I. FTIR data reinforce this distinction: Baikal white nephrite spectra commonly show strong bands around 420, 663, 952, 1064 and 1103 cm−1 36, whereas the Houtaomuga samples are characterised by a slightly different, internally consistent pattern, with dominant absorptions at approximately 415, 543, 680, 1040, 1091 and ~1145 cm−1 (Fig. 12, and Table 2). In addition, Raman spectra of the Houtaomuga artifacts are consistent with tremolite fingerprints, but their peak positions differ from those of the Baikal references reported, most clearly in the low-wavenumber region around 225–232 cm−1 37. Further, in terms of chronology, the Kitoi phase (c. 7650 BP) and the Glazkovo phase (c. 5100 BP) suggest an apparent gap in cultural activity in the Baikal region that overlaps with the Houtaomuga Phase III–IV chronology. Therefore, this apparent hiatus in Baikal relative to active interaction at Houtaomuga does not support jade exchange between the two areas during this period38,39. With clearly defined cultural phasing and a coherent set of spectroscopic and technological observations, the site points to two distinct raw-material pathways within the same community: one linked to shallow mountain nephrite of local or near-regional origin, and the other associated with non-local Xiuyan-type material. This dual pattern provides a clear basis for understanding how multiple procurement and circulation strategies operated concurrently within a single Neolithic community, and offers a concrete reference point for refining models of multi-path raw-material acquisition and jade exchange. Although limited in scale, the raw-material diversity at Houtaomuga is tightly constrained in both chronological and mineralogical terms, making it a focused and instructive case for exploring multi-path jade circulation in Neolithic Northeast Asia.
From a methodological perspective, this study shows that even under a strict prohibition on destructive sampling, the raw materials of early jade artifacts can be preliminarily characterised and their provenance constrained by integrating macroscopic observation, manufacturing-trace analysis, FTIR and Raman spectroscopy. These methods are effective for mineral identification and for distinguishing material groups, but do not resolve the trace-element and rare-earth-element signatures that are often more diagnostic of specific geological sources; analyses by techniques such as LA-ICP-MS would be a valuable next step when sampling conditions permit. The non-destructive framework established here thus provides a methodological reference for future studies of nephrite artifacts at other archaeological sites in Northeast Asia.
